1. Title: Car Evaluation Database 2. Sources: (a) Creator: Marko Bohanec (b) Donors: Marko Bohanec (marko.bohanec@ijs.si) Blaz Zupan (blaz.zupan@ijs.si) (c) Date: June, 1997 3. Past Usage: The hierarchical decision model, from which this dataset is derived, was first presented in M. Bohanec and V. Rajkovic: Knowledge acquisition and explanation for multi-attribute decision making. In 8th Intl Workshop on Expert Systems and their Applications, Avignon, France. pages 59-78, 1988. Within machine-learning, this dataset was used for the evaluation of HINT (Hierarchy INduction Tool), which was proved to be able to completely reconstruct the original hierarchical model. This, together with a comparison with C4.5, is presented in B. Zupan, M. Bohanec, I. Bratko, J. Demsar: Machine learning by function decomposition. ICML-97, Nashville, TN. 1997 (to appear) 4. Relevant Information Paragraph: Car Evaluation Database was derived from a simple hierarchical decision model originally developed for the demonstration of DEX (M. Bohanec, V. Rajkovic: Expert system for decision making. Sistemica 1(1), pp. 145-157, 1990.). The model evaluates cars according to the following concept structure: CAR car acceptability . PRICE overall price . . buying buying price . . maint price of the maintenance . TECH technical characteristics . . COMFORT comfort . . . doors number of doors . . . persons capacity in terms of persons to carry . . . lug_boot the size of luggage boot . . safety estimated safety of the car Input attributes are printed in lowercase. Besides the target concept (CAR), the model includes three intermediate concepts: PRICE, TECH, COMFORT. Every concept is in the original model related to its lower level descendants by a set of examples (for these examples sets see http://www-ai.ijs.si/BlazZupan/car.html). The Car Evaluation Database contains examples with the structural information removed, i.e., directly relates CAR to the six input attributes: buying, maint, doors, persons, lug_boot, safety. Because of known underlying concept structure, this database may be particularly useful for testing constructive induction and structure discovery methods. 5. Number of Instances: 1728 (instances completely cover the attribute space) 6. Number of Attributes: 6 7. Attribute Values: buying v-high, high, med, low maint v-high, high, med, low doors 2, 3, 4, 5-more persons 2, 4, more lug_boot small, med, big safety low, med, high 8. Missing Attribute Values: none 9. Observation:
The dataset contains 1,728 observations, six input features, and one target variable. All variables are currently stored as categorical object data types, which is consistent with the nature of the Car Evaluation dataset. No missing values were identified, therefore no missing value treatment is required.

The original target is noticeably imbalanced. Around 70% of the observations are classified as unacc, approximately 22% as acc, while the good and vgood classes each represent less than 4% of the dataset. As required for this task, I will combine good and vgood into a single Good category before modelling.

#### B1.3 Observations
The input features are evenly distributed across their respective categories, therefore their individual frequency plots do not reveal any major imbalance or unusual pattern. The target variable, however, remains clearly imbalanced, with the majority of cars classified as Unacceptable and a much smaller proportion classified as Good.

The relationship plots provide more useful information. Safety appears to have a strong relationship with the final evaluation, as all cars with Low safety are classified as Unacceptable (it ties to my example in Part A of the report!), while higher safety levels contain considerably larger proportions of Acceptable and Good cars. Passenger capacity also appears important, as cars with a capacity of 2 persons are entirely classified as Unacceptable.

Buying price and maintenance cost also show differences in class proportions, with lower cost categories generally containing more favourable evaluations. Luggage boot size shows some variation in the target distribution, while the number of doors appears to have a weaker relationship with the final class.

These patterns suggest that Safety and Persons may become particularly influential features when the classification models are trained.

I will use this baseline as the starting point for performance evaluation and later compare it with a controlled tree depth, Random Forest, and AdaBoost models.

#### B2.3 Observations

The unrestricted baseline Decision Tree achieved perfect performance on the training data, with all four metrics equal to 1.00. On the unseen testing data, the model also performed very strongly, achieving 99.1% accuracy and a macro F1-score of 0.975.

The small difference between training and testing performance indicates that the full tree has fitted the training data completely, although the reduction in testing performance is relatively minor at this stage. Since the tree was intentionally grown without any depth restriction, I will investigate this further when analysing tree complexity and the bias variance trade off in Section B4.

The strong Precision, Recall, and F1-score also indicate that the model is performing well across the three classes despite the class imbalance.

#### B2.4 Observations

The class level results confirm that the baseline Decision Tree performs very strongly across all three target classes. The Unacceptable class was classified perfectly, with all 242 test observations correctly predicted and Precision, Recall, and F1-score all equal to 1.00.

The remaining errors occurred between the Acceptable and Good classes. Two Acceptable cars were incorrectly classified as Good, while one Good car was classified as Acceptable. This indicates that the model has slightly more difficulty separating these two neighbouring evaluation categories than identifying Unacceptable cars.

The Good class is the most difficult class overall, with the lowest Precision of 0.929 and F1-score of 0.945. This is also the smallest class in the testing dataset, with only 27 observations, which makes its performance particularly important given the class imbalance.

Overall, only three of the 346 testing observations were misclassified, which is consistent with the very high testing accuracy of 99.1%.

B.3.2 Root Impurity Reduction

In [22]:
# Identifying the left and right child nodes of the root
left_child = baseline_dt.tree_.children_left[0]
right_child = baseline_dt.tree_.children_right[0]

# Extracting Gini impurity values for the parent and child nodes
parent_gini = baseline_dt.tree_.impurity[0]
left_gini = baseline_dt.tree_.impurity[left_child]
right_gini = baseline_dt.tree_.impurity[right_child]

# Extracting the number of training observations in each node
parent_samples = baseline_dt.tree_.n_node_samples[0]
left_samples = baseline_dt.tree_.n_node_samples[left_child]
right_samples = baseline_dt.tree_.n_node_samples[right_child]

# Calculating the weighted impurity after the root split
weighted_child_gini = (
    (left_samples / parent_samples) * left_gini +
    (right_samples / parent_samples) * right_gini
)

# Calculating the reduction in Gini impurity achieved by the root split
gini_reduction = parent_gini - weighted_child_gini

print("Parent Gini:", round(parent_gini, 4))
print("Left child Gini:", round(left_gini, 4))
print("Right child Gini:", round(right_gini, 4))
print("Weighted child Gini:", round(weighted_child_gini, 4))
print("Root Gini reduction:", round(gini_reduction, 4))
Parent Gini: 0.4541 Left child Gini: 0.0 Right child Gini: 0.5721 Weighted child Gini: 0.3817 Root Gini reduction: 0.0724

#### B3 Observations

The Decision Tree interpretation shows that Persons is the most important feature at the root of the baseline tree. The first split occurs at persons <= 0.5, which corresponds to separating cars with a capacity of 2 persons from cars that can carry 4 or more persons. All 460 training observations in the 2-person branch are classified as Unacceptable, with a Gini impurity of 0, meaning that this node is completely pure.

The root node has a Gini impurity of 0.4541. After the first split, the weighted impurity of the two child nodes decreases to 0.3817, giving a Gini impurity reduction of 0.0724. This confirms that passenger capacity provides useful information for separating the evaluation classes.

The extracted rules also show that the tree next considers Safety. For cars carrying more than 2 persons, Low safety leads to another completely pure Unacceptable node. For cars with Medium or High safety, the tree continues to consider features such as Buying Price, Maintenance Cost, and Luggage Boot size.

These rules demonstrate the interpretability of Decision Trees, as I can follow each feature based condition from the root to a final prediction. For example, one clear rule learned directly from the training data is: if Persons = 2, then the predicted class is Unacceptable. Another is: if Persons > 2 and Safety = Low, then the predicted class is Unacceptable.

B.4 - Tree Complexity & Bias-Variance Trade-off

 

B.4.1 Testing Different Tree Depths

In [24]:
# Creating lists to store the performance obtained at each tree depth
depths = range(1, 16)
train_accuracy = []
test_accuracy = []
train_f1 = []
test_f1 = []

# Training a separate Decision Tree for each maximum depth
for depth in depths:
    dt = DecisionTreeClassifier(
        criterion='gini',
        max_depth=depth,
        random_state=42
    )
    dt.fit(X_train, y_train)

    # Generating predictions for the training and testing datasets
    y_train_pred = dt.predict(X_train)
    y_test_pred = dt.predict(X_test)

    # Recording Accuracy for each depth
    train_accuracy.append(accuracy_score(y_train, y_train_pred))
    test_accuracy.append(accuracy_score(y_test, y_test_pred))

    # Recording Macro F1-score for each depth
    train_f1.append(f1_score(y_train, y_train_pred, average='macro', zero_division=0))
    test_f1.append(f1_score(y_test, y_test_pred, average='macro', zero_division=0))

# Combining the results into one table
depth_results = pd.DataFrame({
    'Depth': list(depths),
    'Training Accuracy': train_accuracy,
    'Testing Accuracy': test_accuracy,
    'Training Macro F1': train_f1,
    'Testing Macro F1': test_f1
})

# Rounding the results for easier comparison
depth_results.round(3)

B.4.2 Selecting the Optimal Tree Depth

))
Selected maximum depth: 11 Training Accuracy: 0.999 Testing Accuracy: 0.991 Testing Macro F1: 0.975
 

B.4.3 Underfitting, Overfitting and the Bias-Variance Trade-off

 
#### B4 Observations

The depth experiment shows a clear relationship between tree complexity and model performance. At very shallow depths, particularly between depths 1 and 3, both training and testing accuracy are relatively low. These trees are too simple to capture the relationships in the data, which indicates underfitting and high bias.

As the maximum depth increases, both training and testing performance improve considerably. The strongest overall performance was obtained with a maximum depth of 11, which achieved a training accuracy of 99.9%, testing accuracy of 99.1%, and testing Macro F1-score of 0.975.

Beyond this point, increasing the depth provides almost no improvement in testing performance, while training performance eventually reaches 100%. This indicates that additional tree complexity mainly helps the model fit the training data more closely without improving its ability to generalise to unseen observations.

The experiment therefore demonstrates the bias variance trade-off. Shallow trees have higher bias because they are too simple, while increasingly deep trees reduce bias but increase model complexity and the potential for higher variance. In this dataset, the difference between training and testing performance remains small, so there is no evidence of severe overfitting. However, depth 11 provides a suitable balance between predictive performance and unnecessary tree complexity.

B.5 - Random Forest: Bagging Ensemble Learning

 

B.5.1 Random Forest Hyperparameter Tuning

In [28]:
# Setting up the Random Forest classifier
rf_model = RandomForestClassifier(
    random_state=42
)

# Defining the hyperparameter combinations to test
rf_param_grid = {
    'n_estimators': [100, 200, 300],
    'max_depth': [5, 10, 15, None],
    'max_features': ['sqrt', 'log2', None]
}

# Using stratified 5-fold cross-validation to preserve the class proportions
rf_cv = StratifiedKFold(
    n_splits=5,
    shuffle=True,
    random_state=42
)

# Searching for the best Random Forest configuration using Macro F1-score
rf_grid_search = GridSearchCV(
    estimator=rf_model,
    param_grid=rf_param_grid,
    scoring='f1_macro',
    cv=rf_cv,
    n_jobs=-1
)

# Fitting all Random Forest combinations using only the training dataset
rf_grid_search.fit(X_train, y_train)

# Displaying the best hyperparameters and cross-validation performance
print("Best parameters:", rf_grid_search.best_params_)
print("Best cross-validation Macro F1:", round(rf_grid_search.best_score_, 3))

#### B5 Observations

Cross validation identified the best Random Forest configuration as 200 trees, a maximum depth of 15, and all available features considered at each split. The best cross validation Macro F1-score was 0.963.

The optimised Random Forest achieved 99.1% testing accuracy and a Macro F1-score of 0.975. Its confusion matrix was identical to the optimised Decision Tree, with only three misclassified observations. Therefore, Random Forest did not improve the final testing performance for this dataset, although it provided a similarly strong result using an ensemble of trees.

The Out of Bag score was 0.983, corresponding to an OOB error of only 0.017. This provides an additional indication that the Random Forest generalises well to observations that were not used by individual trees during training.

Feature importance identified Safety as the most influential feature overall, followed by Persons, Maintenance Cost, Buying Price, and Luggage Boot size. Although Persons was the root feature in the individual Decision Tree, Random Forest importance considers the accumulated contribution of each feature across all trees and splits, which explains why Safety ranks highest overall.

#### B6.3 Observations

The first AdaBoost weak learner achieved a weighted classification error of 0.300 and received a relatively high learner weight of 1.543. As additional learners were trained, their individual errors generally increased because AdaBoost progressively placed more emphasis on observations that previous learners found difficult to classify.

The later weak learners therefore operate on an increasingly challenging weighted dataset and generally receive less influence in the final ensemble. This demonstrates the sequential nature of boosting, where each learner attempts to improve the mistakes made earlier rather than being trained independently.

B.6.5 Bagging vs Boosting: Final Model Recommendation

 
Based on my experimental results, Bagging through Random Forest is more suitable than Boosting through AdaBoost for the Car Evaluation dataset. Random Forest achieved 99.1% testing accuracy and a Macro F1-score of 0.975, compared with 87.9% accuracy and 0.845 Macro F1 for AdaBoost.

Random Forest also achieved an OOB score of 0.983, providing further evidence that its performance generalises well beyond the individual bootstrap samples used to train its trees. AdaBoost, despite sequentially focusing on observations that previous learners misclassified, produced substantially more classification errors across all three target classes.

Interestingly, Random Forest did not outperform the optimised Decision Tree on the final test set, as both achieved identical performance. However, Random Forest provides the additional benefit of combining many trees rather than relying on a single model, together with OOB evaluation and ensemble based feature importance. Therefore, if selecting an ensemble approach for this problem, I would recommend Random Forest over AdaBoost.
